sources.title: Linda Colley, “The Sea Around Us” (2006).
sources.citation: Linda Colley, “The Sea Around Us,” New York Review of Books, 22 June 2006, review of Bernard Bailyn, Atlantic History: Concept and Contours, and Carla Gardina Pestana, The English Atlantic in an Age of Revolution, 1640–1661.

verification.note: Fresh selected publisher HTML: section 1 final paragraphs on Atlantic unity; section 2 final paragraphs on Asia and global connections. The review explicitly distinguishes its two books. Colley credits Bailyn’s contribution while objecting to his stronger claims of a discrete Atlantic whole. Her selected argument, rather than the unread whole of Bailyn’s 2005 book, supports the criticism. Full original HTML saved; no printed-page collation.

sources.title: Bernard Bailyn, “An American Tragedy” (1995).
sources.citation: Bernard Bailyn, “An American Tragedy,” New York Review of Books, 5 October 1995, 14–16, review of Colin G. Calloway, The American Revolution in Indian Country: Crisis and Diversity in Native American Communities.

verification.note: Fresh selected publisher HTML: opening assessment, village-study qualification, and final contextual argument. Bailyn acknowledges the documented devastation and nuances while criticizing the broad interpretive framing. The reviewer’s judgments are attributed to Bailyn, not adopted as a verdict on Calloway or Indigenous history. Calloway’s full book and any reply unread; no printed-page collation. Full original HTML saved.

sources.title: Bernard Bailyn, The Ideological Origins of the American Revolution, enlarged edition (1992), selected foreword.
sources.citation: Bernard Bailyn, The Ideological Origins of the American Revolution, enlarged edition (Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 1992), foreword signed 1967, especially xii.

verification.note: Fresh 1992 scan: title/imprint, enlarged-edition preface v–viii, and foreword ix–xvi; xii visually checked against the actual page image. On xii Bailyn identifies a set of British historical studies used in reconstructing colonial radical and opposition thought, explicitly including Pocock. This is the later witness of the foreword signed 1967, not a collation against an original 1967 copy. Robbins and other named scholars, plus Jane N. Garrett’s research and Carol S. Thorne’s assistance, retain separate credit. Whole book and Pocock originals unread.

sources.title: Jack Rakove, “Some Thoughts about My Mentor” (2020/2021).
sources.citation: Jack Rakove, “Some Thoughts about My Mentor,” The Docket / Law and History Review, posted 23 December 2020, updated 6 January 2021.

verification.note: Fresh selected named scholarly reading: the paragraph beginning the discussion of Ideological Origins and the two following paragraphs. Rakove specifically identifies Morgan’s Stamp Act research as a basis Bailyn extended. This is Rakove’s substantive reconstruction; the original Morgan studies and their complete authorship/edition histories were not newly read. The route does not claim exclusive authorship or sole intellectual origin. Rakove’s own mentoring testimony is separate and lacks an individual graph endpoint.

hc173_bernard_bailyn_1.note: Fresh selected AHA primary HTML: paragraphs discussing Braudel’s three temporal layers, their attempted integration and historical narration; notes 8 and 10. Note 10 explicitly combines agreement with Stone and methodological differences, and says Stone was read after the draft. Delivery in December 1981 remains distinct from AHR publication in February 1982. The 1951 Braudel review, complete Stone essay and complete address were not freshly read. Local direct AHA retrieval returned 403; the actual substantive HTML was read through the web tool and its response saved under ignored raw/. Annual-report scan was discoverable but local retrieval and screenshot failed; no visual collation claimed.
